## Four promising datasets inspected

These cover **cover-crop implementation, field experiments, irrigation methods, and agricultural climate metrics**. Details below come from inspected catalog records; linked downloads were not fetched.

### 1. Chesapeake Bay conservation tillage and cover crops
**Publisher:** U.S. Geological Survey, using practices reported to the Chesapeake Bay Program.  
**Source:** [DOI: 10.5066/P9SRZS8P](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P); catalog ID `USGS_5b3bb606e4b040769c18bdc9`.

- **Geography:** Chesapeake Bay watershed; estimates allocated to NHDPlus V1 catchments.
- **Observation years:** Cover crops: **2002, 2012**. Conservation tillage: **1985, 1992, 2002, 2012**—not a continuous annual series.
- **Formats/access:** Catalog distributions labeled XML, including original metadata and a DOI access page. Reviewed watershed-level snapshots use CSV files.
- **Dictionary/terms:** No separate dictionary surfaced; metadata marks access public but supplies no explicit license.
- **Uncertainties:** Spatially allocated reported practices, not direct catchment measurements. The reviewed cover-crop measure is allocated implementation area, **not an adoption rate**. Only the narrow historical watershed summaries are available for analysis here.

### 2. Late-seeded cover crops in a semiarid environment
**Publisher:** USDA Agricultural Research Service.  
**Source:** [DOI: 10.15482/USDA.ADC/26836453.v1](https://doi.org/10.15482/USDA.ADC/26836453.v1).

- **Geography:** Research farm near Mandan, North Dakota; rainfed, semiarid conditions.
- **Observation period:** Structured metadata says **August 2008–May 2011**, while the description says a three-year study initiated in 2009; reconcile against files.
- **Formats/access:** XLSX treatment, management, biomass and subsequent-crop yield files; CSV metadata also advertised.
- **Dictionary/terms:** Explicit XLSX and [CSV data dictionary](https://ndownloader.figshare.com/files/49752696); **CC0**.
- **Uncertainties:** Distribution listing was truncated; schema, units and actual file availability remain unverified. This is a local experiment, not regional adoption data.

### 3. California Statewide Irrigation Systems Methods Survey
**Publisher:** California Department of Water Resources.  
**Identifier:** `c4201e7a-099f-4eff-859f-3e4521edb370`.

- **Geography:** California; respondents reported their main county, crop acreages and irrigation methods.
- **Survey years:** **1991, 2001, 2010, 2016, 2021**; advertised files reference 2021.
- **Formats/access:** [Survey spreadsheet](https://data.cnra.ca.gov/dataset/189fa7df-b186-4e77-8bf6-617e5bebc93e/resource/3778f493-5184-404e-8ff6-f098f7a92d23/download/2021_statewide_irrigation_methods_survey.xls), labeled XLSM although its extension is `.xls`.
- **Dictionary/terms:** Neither dictionary nor explicit license surfaced; public access claimed.
- **Uncertainties:** County output detail and historical-file coverage unverified. Rice-only, non-irrigation and livestock-only growers were excluded.

### 4. California specialty-crop agroclimate metrics
**Publisher:** USDA Agricultural Research Service.  
**Source:** [DOI: 10.15482/USDA.ADC/26517244.v1](https://doi.org/10.15482/USDA.ADC/26517244.v1).

- **Geography/period:** California, **1981–2020**.
- **Formats/access:** ZIP advertised with MATLAB code, tables, products and geographic boundary files.
- **Dictionary/terms:** No standalone dictionary surfaced; **CC BY 4.0**.
- **Uncertainties:** Exact spatial resolution, metric units and archive contents require inspection.

**Search coverage:** I checked reviewed analytical availability, then searched Data.gov for “cover crops,” “irrigation,” and “climate agricultural practices,” reviewing the first five results each and inspecting these four records. This is targeted discovery, not exhaustive coverage. Next steps are dictionary/file inspection and verification of matching geography and years before combining sources.

Drought-adaptation research, not regional monitoring. | **PDF final report** and HTML page. Catalog does not establish availability of machine-readable raw measurements. |
| **USGS — [Estimated Monthly Irrigation Water Use, 2015](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9FDLY8P)** · `USGS:5ff7acf4d34ea5387df03d73` | Conterminous U.S., including the West; monthly **2015**, HUC12 watersheds | **Modeled estimates and research code.** IWUEDD downscales/disaggregates annual county estimates into monthly watershed withdrawals and consumptive use. These are **not independently measured monthly watershed totals**. Description explicitly includes scripts and replication resources. | DOI route and XML metadata; underlying output formats, programming language, and code license unverified. |
| **USGS — [Drought and southwestern pronghorn trajectories](https://doi.org/10.5066/F76972HS)** · `USGS:59d256ece4b05fe04cc235d2` | Arizona, New Mexico, Utah, western Texas; historical dates incompletely specified; projections **through 2090** | **Historical survey/climate inputs plus Bayesian projections** under higher/lower CO₂ scenarios. Drought-impact ecology—not irrigation-demand projections or future observations. | DOI route and XML metadata; underlying data formats unverified. |

### Coverage and remaining unknowns

- Searched four keyword combinations: “drought irrigation,” “western irrigation,” “drought projections western,” and “irrigation code.” Reviewed first-page results; this is **selective, not exhaustive**.

- None has verified observation-query access here. Next steps are to inspect publisher documentation, schemas, units, code dependencies, and reuse terms before selecting or combining files. Metadata modification/harvest dates are **not observation dates**.

dataset.title: Data release for Influence of multi-decadal land use, irrigation practices and climate on riparian corridors across the Upper Missouri River headwaters basin, Montana
dataset.description: The Upper Missouri River headwaters (UMH) basin (36 400 km2 ) depends on its river corridors to support irrigated agriculture and world-class trout fisheries. We evaluated trends (1984–2016) in riparian wetness, an indicator of the riparian condition, in peak irrigation months (June, July and August) for 158 km2 of riparian area across the basin using the Landsat normalized difference wetness index (NDWI). We found that 8 of the 19 riparian reaches across the basin showed a significant drying trend over this period, including all three basin outlet reaches along the Jefferson, Madison and Gallatin rivers. The influence of upstream climate was quantified using per reach random forest regressions. Much of the interannual variability in the NDWI was explained by climate, especially by drought indices and annual precipitation, but the significant temporal drying trends persisted in the NDWI–climate model residuals, indicating that trends were not entirely attributable to climate. Over the same period we documented a basin-wide shift from 9 % of agriculture irrigated with center-pivot irrigation to 50 % irrigated with center-pivot irrigation. Riparian reaches with a drying trend had a greater increase in the total area with center-pivot irrigation (within reach and upstream from the reach) relative to riparian reaches without such a trend (p < 0.05). The drying trend, however, did not extend to river discharge. Over the same period, stream gages (n = 7) showed a positive correlation with riparian wetness (p < 0.05) but no trend in summer river discharge, suggesting that riparian areas may be more sensitive to changes in irrigation return flows relative to river discharge. Identifying trends in riparian vegetation is a critical precursor for enhancing the resiliency of river systems and associated riparian corridors.

dataset.title: Impact of Drought on Southwestern Pronghorn Population Trends and Predicted Trajectories in the Southwest in the Face of Climate Change
dataset.description:
Climate often drives ungulate population dynamics, and as climates change, some areas may become unsuitable for species persistence. Unraveling the relationships between climate and population dynamics, and projecting them across time, advances ecological understanding that informs and steers sustainable conservation for species. Using pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) as an ecological model, we used a Bayesian approach to analyze long-term population, precipitation, and temperature data from 18 subpopulations in the southwestern United States. We determined which long-term (12 and 24 months) or short-term (gestation trimester and lactation period) climatic conditions best predicted annual rate of population growth (λ). We used these predictions to project population trends through 2090. Projections incorporated downscaled climatic data matched to pronghorn range for each population, given a high and a lower atmospheric CO2 concentration scenario. Since the 1990s, 15 of the pronghorn subpopulations declined in abundance. Sixteen subpopulations demonstrated a significant relationship between precipitation and λ, and in 13 of these, temperature was also significant. Precipitation predictors of λ were highly seasonal, with lactation being the most important period, followed by early and late gestation. The influence of temperature on λ was less seasonal than precipitation, and lacked a clear temporal pattern. The climatic projections indicated that all of these pronghorn subpopulations would experience increased temperatures, while the direction and magnitude of precipitation had high subpopulation-specific variation. Models predicted that nine subpopulations would be extirpated or approaching extirpation by 2090. Results were consistent across both atmospheric CO2 concentration scenarios, indicating robustness of trends irrespective of climatic severity. In the southwestern United States, the climate underpinning pronghorn subpopulations is shifting, making conditions increasingly inhospitable to pronghorn persistence. This realization informs and steers conservation and management decisions for pronghorn in North America, while exemplifying how similar research can aid ungulates inhabiting arid regions and confronting similar circumstances elsewhere.

datasets.title: S&T Project 1780 Final Report: Determining Impacts of Long-Term Use of Reverse Osmosis Concentrate as Drip Irrigation Water Source on Atriplex species, Soil Characteristics and Microbial Communities
datasets.description: Drought in the Western U.S. has increased interest in non-traditional irrigation sources such as brackish groundwater. RO can be used to reduce salinity but can pose disposal issues for saline concentrates. A potential safe and beneficial use of saline concentrate is irrigation of halophytic species for livestock fodder. Objectives were to determine the impacts of brackish irrigation water on soil chemical properties, soil microbial communities, and plant germination/growth. Field studies included Atriplex plantings irrigated at different salinity concentrations. Soils were analyzed for EC, ion concentration, pH, and carbon/nitrogen. Next-Generation Sequencing was conducted to assess soil microbial communities. Greenhouse studies involved planting 2 species of Atriplex in clay or sand soils irrigated with water at various salinities. Plants were measured for germination, height, IR, and SPAD. Soil EC increased with distance from the irrigation emitter. Ion concentrations, pH and carbon/nitrogen ratios varied; soil microbe communities shifted but were not statistically significantly. Germination was significant by species, soil type, and irrigation treatment. Higher salinities did not significantly affect plant height or SPAD, but significantly increased IR. Further studies are needed to develop a better understanding and management practices for safe and effective use of saline concentrate to grow halophytes for livestock fodder.

datasets.title: Data release for Influence of multi-decadal land use, irrigation practices and climate on riparian corridors across the Upper Missouri River headwaters basin, Montana
datasets.description: The Upper Missouri River headwaters (UMH) basin (36 400 km2 ) depends on its river corridors to support irrigated agriculture and world-class trout fisheries. We evaluated trends (1984–2016) in riparian wetness, an indicator of the riparian condition, in peak irrigation months (June, July and August) for 158 km2 of riparian area across the basin using the Landsat normalized difference wetness index (NDWI). We found that 8 of the 19 riparian reaches across the basin showed a significant drying trend over this period, including all three basin outlet reaches along the Jefferson, Madison and Gallatin rivers. The influence of upstream climate was quantified using per reach random forest regressions. Much of the interannual variability in the NDWI was explained by climate, especially by drought indices and annual precipitation, but the significant temporal drying trends persisted in the NDWI–climate model residuals, indicating that trends were not entirely attributable to climate. Over the same period we documented a basin-wide shift from 9 % of agriculture irrigated with center-pivot irrigation to 50 % irrigated with center-pivot irrigation. Riparian reaches with a drying trend had a greater increase in the total area with center-pivot irrigation (within reach and upstream from the reach) relative to riparian reaches without such a trend (p < 0.05). The drying trend, however, did not extend to river discharge. Over the same period, stream gages (n = 7) showed a positive correlation with riparian wetness (p < 0.05) but no trend in summer river discharge, suggesting that riparian areas may be more sensitive to changes in irrigation return flows relative to river discharge. Identifying trends in riparian vegetation is a critical precursor for enhancing the resiliency of river systems and associated riparian corridors.

## Maryland annual average temperature, 1985–2012

**The reviewed series starts at 54.8°F in 1985 and ends at 57.5°F in 2012—a rise of 2.7°F.** This is an endpoint difference, not a climate-trend estimate.

The registered measure is the **mean of monthly statewide average temperatures, January–December**, in degrees Fahrenheit.

| Year | °F | Year | °F |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| 1985 | 54.8 | 1999 | 55.7 |
| 1986 | 54.6 | 2000 | 54.1 |
| 1987 | 54.7 | 2001 | 55.3 |
| 1988 | 53.7 | 2002 | 56.3 |
| 1989 | 53.5 | 2003 | 53.9 |
| 1990 | 56.6 | 2004 | 55.2 |
| 1991 | 56.5 | 2005 | 55.2 |
| 1992 | 53.5 | 2006 | 56.5 |
| 1993 | 54.2 | 2007 | 55.7 |

### Is that enough to establish a climate trend?

**No—not by itself.** Comparing two years ignores the intervening annual variability and is sensitive to the endpoints chosen. Establishing a trend requires analysis of the full time series and its uncertainty, rather than treating the 2.7°F difference as a trend estimate. This does **not** establish that there is no warming trend; it means the endpoint comparison alone cannot establish one or attribute its cause.

**Estimated cover-crop implementation increased from 481.509 km² in 2002 to 1,770.5665 km² in 2012**, a net increase of **1,289.0575 km²** across the Chesapeake Bay watershed.

| Observation year | Estimated cover-crop area |
|---|---:|
| 2002 | 481.509 km² |
| 2012 | 1,770.5665 km² |
| Change, 2012 minus 2002 | **+1,289.0575 km²** |

### How the estimates were produced
According to the [USGS data release](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P):

1. The six watershed states—New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Delaware, West Virginia, and Virginia—reported implementation of these best management practices to the Chesapeake Bay Program.
2. Estimates supplied to USGS were originally expressed in **acres per land–river modeling segment**.
3. Those reported areas were spatially distributed to agricultural land-use cells in the National Land Cover Dataset, then summed into **NHDPlus version 1 catchments**.
4. The watershed totals above come from the reviewed `covcrop.csv` data, aggregated across **50,871 catchments**. Its registered measure is “allocated area of reported cover-crop implementation,” expressed in **square kilometres—not acres or hectares**.

These are **spatially allocated estimates of reported practices**, not direct measurements of cover crops in every catchment or a percentage of farms adopting them. The comparison establishes an increase between two endpoints; with only 2002 and 2012 available for this measure, it does not establish a continuous annual trend or explain why implementation increased.

Source: USGS/Chesapeake Bay Program, DOI [10.5066/P9SRZS8P](https://doi.org/10.5066/P9SRZS8P), `covcrop.csv`. Verified change-result evidence ID: `f1d93ff105cc4d8e8beac71e81e3e0ef`.
